notes.meaning: Eliphaz challenges Job to call out and see if anyone will take his side. He asks whether any angel or godly person would ever support Job's angry complaints against God. In his mind, no true servant of the Lord has ever suffered like this without being guilty of serious sin.

Fretting in anger and jealousy only destroys the person who holds onto it. Eliphaz warns that bitter resentment eats away at a person's life and brings sudden ruin. He is hinting that Job's anger against God proves he is acting like a foolish man.

Eliphaz describes seeing a wicked man who seemed firmly planted in wealth and security. Yet disaster arrived suddenly, showing that God's curse was resting on the man's home all along. He points to this to suggest that Job's sudden downfall follows the very same pattern.

The children of the foolish man are left without safety and receive no help when crushed in the city court. In ancient times, the city gate was where legal cases were decided and judgments were handed down. Eliphaz cruelly uses this picture to remind Job of the tragic death of his own children.

Desperate and hungry people strip away all the crops of the wicked man, taking grain even from among the thorn bushes. Greedy raiders swallow up his wealth until nothing remains. Eliphaz is pointing directly to how raiders had just carried off Job's own livestock and riches.

Hardship does not just grow up out of the dirt like a wild weed. Troubles are not random accidents of nature or bad luck. Eliphaz argues that pain comes because of human sin under God's righteous rule.

Human beings are born into a fallen, sinful world, so trouble is their natural share in life. Hardship follows human life just as surely as hot sparks fly upward from a blazing fire. Because suffering is the common lot of mankind, Eliphaz thinks Job should endure it without complaining so bitterly.

Eliphaz gives Job the advice he claims he would follow if he were in Job's shoes. Instead of arguing or complaining, he would humbly seek God in prayer and place his whole case into the Lord's hands. It is good counsel to pray in times of distress, though Eliphaz wrongly implies Job has refused to do so.

God does marvelous things that are far beyond human understanding and too numerous to count. His power is limitless, and His wise plans cannot be fully searched out by human minds. Therefore, a person in trouble can safely trust such an almighty God to help.

God shows His quiet power and goodness by sending rain onto the earth and watering the open fields. People often take rain for granted, but it is a wonderful gift that keeps all living things alive. The God who cares for the dry ground can also refresh a broken life.

The Lord lifts up those who are lowly and brings grieving people into safety. He has the power to reverse human fortunes in a moment. Eliphaz suggests that if Job will only humble himself, God will lift him out of his deep sorrow.

God breaks up the clever plots of crafty people so their hands cannot carry out their schemes. No matter how carefully wicked people plan to get their way, God stays in complete control. Human scheming can never defeat the purposes of God.

God catches the worldly-wise in their own cunning traps, sweeping away their plans before they can succeed. Those who plot against others often end up falling into the very pits they dug. The apostle Paul later quotes this verse in the New Testament to show that human wisdom is nothing compared to God's.

Cunning schemers become so confused that they stumble in broad daylight as if it were the middle of the night. God clouds their judgment so that they make foolish blunders even in simple matters. Worldly cleverness cannot guide anyone safely without the light of God.

God rescues the poor from the sharp words of the powerful, which cut like a deadly sword. He protects the weak and defenseless from being crushed by mighty bullies. When oppressors use lies and slander to destroy others, God steps in to save.

When God delivers the oppressed, the poor receive fresh hope that they are not forgotten. At the same time, wicked oppressors are silenced and shamed by God's justice. Seeing God act on behalf of the needy gives quiet courage to everyone who trusts Him.

Eliphaz says that a person corrected by God is truly blessed, so Job should not despise the Almighty's discipline. He teaches that God uses painful trials as a loving Father to correct His children and keep them from worse sins. While this principle is true, Eliphaz misapplies it by assuming Job's disaster was sent to correct hidden sins.

God may cause a painful wound, but He also tenderly bandages and heals it. His blows are not meant to destroy His children, but to bring them to repentance so He can restore them. The same loving hand that allows the affliction will bring the cure.

Eliphaz promises that God will repeatedly rescue Job from troubles as often as they come. The phrase six and then seven is a Hebrew poetic way of saying through countless or complete troubles. No matter how many hardships arrive, God will keep real harm from destroying the righteous person.

When food runs out and famine strikes, God will preserve the life of His servant. In times of war, the Lord will shield him from the deadly strike of the sword. God is fully able to protect His people even during widespread disasters.

God promises shelter from the whipping blows of cruel gossip, lies, and slander. Even when destruction sweeps through the land, a person who rests in God will not live in terror. God guards both the good name and the peace of mind of those who trust Him.

A person under God's protection can face ruin and starvation with cheerful confidence instead of dread. They do not need to live in fear of dangerous wild animals. True trust in God gives a quiet heart even when surrounded by threats.

Eliphaz poetically says that the stones in the field and the wild beasts will be at peace with the righteous man. Rocks will not ruin the fertility of his soil, and dangerous animals will not harm his herds. When a person walks in fellowship with God, the surrounding creation works for his good rather than his harm.

Job is promised that his home will be safe and filled with peace. When he inspects his tent, his fields, and his animals, he will find nothing missing or out of order. God's watchful care extends to every detail of daily life.

Eliphaz assures Job that his family line will flourish again and his descendants will become as numerous as blades of grass. Even though Job had just lost all ten of his children, Eliphaz holds out the hope of a rebuilt family. In ancient times, a large and thriving family was seen as a special sign of God's blessing.

The righteous person will live a full, complete life and come to the grave in a ripe old age. Just as bundles of golden wheat are gathered into the barn at the proper harvest time, a godly person dies at the right season when their life's work is finished. Death for the believer is not a tragic defeat, but a peaceful gathering home.

Eliphaz concludes by saying that he and his friends have carefully studied these truths through long observation and know they are reliable. He urges Job to listen to this wisdom and take it to heart for his own good. His advice contained many true principles, yet his self-confident certainty blinded him to Job's real situation.
